source: Li and Kingsford (2026) Means-Ends Analysis Helps LLMs Plan in Continuous-State Domains (MEDAKA, arXiv 2610.24928)
finding: A structured prompt built on Newell and Simon means-ends analysis (derive the goal, find the blocker, push a subgoal on a stack, track state) beat chain of thought and AoT+ on a fluid-mixing planning testbed for most of 7 models.
numbers: LiquidWorld, 189 problems, 3 rollouts each, thinking mode off, temp 0. Pass@1 total CoT / AoT+ / MEDAKA: Claude Sonnet 4.6 77.8/85.0/94.5; Gemini 3 Flash 65.6/71.6/82.0; GPT-5.4 74.3/78.5/78.5 (tie); GPT-4o 25.7/19.8/36.9; Llama 3.3 70B 26.6/17.6/40.6; Gemma4 4B 55.7/52.7/61.0; Gemma4 2B 26.3/23.8/30.5. Token cost 1.8 to 3.8 times CoT median.
quote: when blocked, the LLM derives a subgoal that resolves the blocker, with deferred subgoals pushed onto a subgoal stack
limits: Read through a page-fetch summary, not the raw PDF. Single-turn prompts only, no external verifier. Testbed is a controlled toy (fully specified, deterministic). Ablations on only 2 models. Preprint dated 18 Oct 2026, not peer reviewed, no replication yet.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of MEA inside a prompt. Gain is large on nonlinear and multi-goal problems and absent for the strongest model on one tag. Shows the stack-of-blockers idea (S6 operator choice) can pay, but it costs about 2-4x tokens, so G7 (equal-token comparison) must be checked.

source: Li and Kingsford (2026) MEDAKA ablations and failure modes (arXiv 2610.24928)
finding: Removing the recursive decomposition module or the state-tracking module each cost points; the recursive part mattered more on Gemini. Weak models still failed by guessing numbers, drifting state and breaking coupled constraints.
numbers: Pass@1 Claude / Gemini: full 94.5/82.0; no state tracking 90.5 (-4.0)/76.0 (-6.0); no recursive module 91.0 (-3.5)/75.1 (-6.9). Nonlinear tag Claude CoT 33.3, AoT+ 55.3, MEDAKA 87.4. Distractor tag GPT-4o 10.7/7.1/42.9. GPT-5.4 nonlinear 28.9/49.1/46.5 (MEDAKA not best). MEDAKA pass@1 beat CoT pass@3 on 4 of 7 models.
limits: No subgoal-stack-only ablation. Neither method helped Gemma4 2B on distractor and multi-goal tags. Authors say open models lack nonlinear ability.
agent_relevance: Both parts (explicit state record, recursive subgoal) earn their keep, but by a few points. A state record is cheap code. The failure mode of state drift argues for code-held state, not model-held state.

source: Thinking Forward and Backward: Effective Backward Planning with Large Language Models (arXiv 2411.01790)
finding: LLMs plan worse backward than forward on all 4 tested domains, even where backward search is computationally easier. Planning in the flipped direction (turn the problem around, then flip the plan back) with self-verification lifted success by 4 to 24 points.
numbers: GPT-4o. Forward vs backward success: undirected graph 82.5 vs 76.7; directed graph 38.5 vs 29.7; array transformation 67.5 vs 62.2; Blocksworld 39.5 vs 20.5. Fwd-Flip vs Fwd (200 trials, M=6 attempts): undirected 93.5 vs 82.5; directed 86.5 vs 69.5; Blocksworld 48.5 vs 39.5; array 56.0 vs 50.0.
quote: the LLM consistently plans worse in the backward direction
limits: Read through a page-fetch summary. Small fixed sizes (10-12 node graphs, 4 blocks). At 1 attempt, Fwd-Flip is slightly worse than Fwd on Blocksworld; the gain needs several attempts. GPT-3.5 always judged its own plan correct, giving near 0 on Blocksworld. When the model chose its own direction it picked the easier one only 60 to 78 percent of the time.
agent_relevance: Pure backward chaining from the goal is a weaker default for an LLM than forward. Use backward as a second attempt with a code check (G2, G3), never as the single route. Direction choice should be made by code, not by the model.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) LAMBADA: Backward Chaining for Automated Reasoning in Natural Language (ACL 2023, arXiv 2212.13894)
finding: A backward-chaining loop made of four few-shot LM modules (fact check, rule selection, goal decomposition, sign agreement) beat chain of thought and forward Selection-Inference on deep proofs, with far fewer model calls.
numbers: PaLM 540B. Relative label-accuracy gain on ProofWriter-PUD Depth-5: +44% over CoT and +56% over Selection-Inference; PrOntoQA Depth-5 +37% over CoT and +113% over SI; ParaRules +43% over CoT. Inference calls: 3.8x fewer than SI at Depth-1, 11.8x fewer at Depth-5. Fact Check accuracy 0.94 with one fact selected, near perfect with two.
limits: Logical deduction over text rules, not state-changing planning. One model family (PaLM). Gains are relative, not absolute.
agent_relevance: Goal-directed decomposition into small checked sub-calls cuts search blow-up for deduction. Supports a code-driven goal stack with the model filling narrow slots (S6/O5).

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) LAMBADA forward vs backward analysis (section 5.3, appendix B.3)
finding: Forward chaining wastes inference: sampled forward steps contained no redundant facts only 29 percent of the time, and forward search gets harder as depth grows. Backward CoT alone, without the modular design, did not clearly beat forward CoT on label accuracy.
numbers: Selection-Inference with 5 inferred facts: 29% all unique, 7% all identical, 10% only two unique (read from figure text). Forward and backward CoT label accuracy comparable on ProofWriter; CoT made correct chains only 28 percent of the time at higher depth in one analysis.
limits: Figure-derived percentages from extracted text may be imperfect. PaLM only.
agent_relevance: Direction alone is not the active ingredient; structure (small, separately checkable steps) is. This matches our rule that the program decides and the model fills one slot.

source: Lee and Hwang (2025) SymBa: Symbolic Backward Chaining for Structured Natural Language Reasoning (NAACL 2025, arXiv 2402.12806)
finding: LAMBADA and least-to-most prompting are incomplete backward chainers (they lack backtracking and binding propagation from SLD resolution). Putting a symbolic SLD solver in control and calling the LLM only for missing facts beat both on 7 benchmarks.
numbers: Average answer accuracy on one model across benchmarks: SymBa 79.8, least-to-most 71.5, LAMBADA 69.7. Ablation: without backtracking 76.3. Without binding propagation the baselines scored 0.0 on the relational task in the ablation table. Four runs per benchmark, 95% confidence for boldface.
quote: the solver controls the proof process, and the LLM is only called when the solver requires new information
limits: Table columns were garbled in text extraction, so per-model numbers are not recorded. Token use was several times higher than LAMBADA. Deductive, relational and arithmetic tasks only.
agent_relevance: Strong support for our design: code owns the goal stack and backtracking, the model only supplies facts. A model-run goal stack loses completeness (no backtrack), which MEA-style prompts silently inherit.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam and Kambhampati (2025) Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2405.04776)
finding: Worked-example prompts for Blocksworld help only when they match the problem class very narrowly. A domain-wide procedure shown by example (unstack everything, then rebuild) gave less gain and did not generalize to taller stacks.
numbers: 261 table-to-stack instances, accuracy GPT-4-Turbo / Claude-3-Opus / GPT-4. Zero-shot 19.1/9.96/3.83; zero-shot CoT 21/10.34/4.98; progression-proof CoT 15.3/4.59/6.89; Blocksworld universal algorithm 37.1/37.1/51.3; stacking-specific prompt 40.6/24.5/59.3. Self-consistency lowered accuracy.
quote: improvements quickly deteriorate as the size n of the query-specified stack grows past the size of stacks shown in the examples
limits: Few-shot demos of a procedure, not a code-held procedure. Single-run style accuracy.
agent_relevance: Showing the model a goal-reduction recipe in context does not give it the algorithm; it copies the pattern and fails out of distribution. The recipe (difference table, stack) should live in code.

source: Stechly et al. (2025) Chain of Thoughtlessness: synthetic domains table (CoinFlip, letter tasks, arithmetic)
finding: Across scalable extra domains, CoT gains were large at small size and fell as the number of reasoning steps rose; a prompt with an incorrect reasoning trace scored almost as well as a correct one on CoinFlip.
numbers: GPT-4-Turbo accuracy, zero-shot / zero-shot CoT / manual CoT: CoinFlip 56.38/95.71/98.89; LastLetterConcat 10.00/52.54/51.06; LastVowelConcat 5.75/N/A/27.00; FirstLetter-type 1.81/N/A/26.00; Arithmetic 24.13/56.12/50.43. Incorrect CoT on CoinFlip 96.76.
limits: Authors' own scalable variants. Incorrect-CoT run on a subset only. Not a planning task in the strict sense.
agent_relevance: Step-by-step text does not encode a procedure that the model then executes faithfully. Supports G2 and G3: trust only checked output, not narrated reasoning.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench: An Extensible Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Planning and Reasoning about Change (arXiv 2206.10498)
finding: GPT-4 solves about a third of Blocksworld plan-generation instances and drops sharply when predicate names are obfuscated, which points to pattern matching over planning.
numbers: 600 instances each. Plan generation: GPT-4 206/600 (34.3%), Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%). Cost-optimal planning GPT-4 198/600 (33%). Plan verification GPT-4 191/600 (31.8%). Replanning GPT-4 461/600 (76.8%). Mystery Blocksworld deceptive GPT-4 26/600 (4.3%); randomized 12/600 (2%).
limits: GPT-4 of early 2023, one-shot prompts. Later models score far higher (see c11).
agent_relevance: Baseline showing plain LLMs do not do means-ends reasoning over arbitrary operators. The obfuscation test is a ready check on whether our MEA scaffold generalizes or just pattern matches (G3).

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) Position: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks (ICML 2024, arXiv 2402.01817)
finding: Autonomously, about 12 percent of GPT-4 plans are executable and goal-reaching. Letting the LLM propose and external critics (a plan validator) send back errors lifts results a lot where the LLM can propose plausible candidates and little where it cannot.
numbers: Autonomous GPT-4 about 12% valid plans on average. With VAL back-prompting: Blocksworld 82% within 15 rounds, Logistics 70%, Mystery Blocksworld about 10%. Travel planning benchmark: best prompting strategies 0.7% on GPT-3.5-Turbo; LLM-Modulo with critics about 6x the baseline within 10 back-prompting cycles.
limits: Position paper; numbers are reported from other papers by the same group. Needs a sound verifier and a domain model, which many tasks lack.
agent_relevance: The generate-and-test loop with a code verifier is the form of planning that works. Mystery Blocksworld at 10% warns that the loop fails when proposals are poor, so MEA proposals need diversity (G4) and checking (G2).

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of OpenAI o1 on PlanBench (arXiv 2409.13373)
finding: o1-preview nearly saturates plain Blocksworld but loses a lot on obfuscated domains and on longer plans, and is hundreds of times slower and pricier than a classical planner.
numbers: 600 instances each. Blocksworld zero-shot: o1-preview 587/600 (97.8%), o1-mini 340/600 (56.6%), Fast Downward 100%. Mystery Blocksworld zero-shot o1-preview 317/600 (52.8%), o1-mini 115/600 (19.1%); one-shot 247/600 (41.6%). Randomized Mystery zero-shot 224/600 (37.3%). Larger problems (110 instances, 6-20 blocks, 20-40 steps): 23.63%. Unsolvable instances flagged correctly 27% on Blocksworld. Best non-reasoning LLM on Blocksworld 62.6% (Llama 3.1 405B); no LLM above 5% on Mystery. Cost per 100 instances: o1-preview 42.12 dollars; time 40 to 111 s versus 0.265 s for Fast Downward.
limits: Read through a page-fetch summary. o1 models only; later reasoning models not covered here.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models fix easy planning but still fall with obfuscation and plan length, which is where operator-difference reasoning matters. A classical solver called by code beats model deliberation on cost and accuracy.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking (Apple, arXiv 2506.06941), via the public page and two commentaries
finding: Reasoning models were tested on Tower of Hanoi, River Crossing, Blocks World and Checker Jumping at growing size. Three regimes: standard models win on easy sizes, thinking models win at medium, both collapse at high size. Giving the model the explicit Hanoi algorithm did not stop the collapse.
numbers: The page gives no numbers. Commentary c14 states that Claude 3.7 Sonnet-Thinking given the optimal Hanoi algorithm still collapsed. Specific size thresholds were not verified in this session.
quote: fail to use explicit algorithms and reason inconsistently across puzzles
limits: The PDF could not be opened (fetch timed out and downloads were truncated), so exact thresholds are not recorded. Disputed by c13, c14, c15.
agent_relevance: The algorithm-given result is the key one for us: a model told the recursive subgoal procedure still could not execute long runs reliably. Supports having code run the goal stack.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (arXiv 2506.09250)
finding: Much of the reported Hanoi collapse is an output-length and format artifact, and the River Crossing failures include mathematically impossible instances. Asking for a program instead of a move list gave high accuracy on 15 disks.
numbers: Hanoi needs 2^N - 1 moves; at 10 tokens per move the 64,000-token limit allows about N = 12-13; reported collapse before N = 9 is earlier than that limit. River Crossing with boat capacity 3 has no solution for N greater than 5, yet N >= 6 instances were scored as failures. Prompt: output a Lua function that prints the solution, 15 disks; Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3, Gemini 2.5 all gave very high accuracy in under 5,000 tokens.
quote: models are making a decision to terminate output before actually reaching their context window limits
limits: Short note, preliminary tests, no table of accuracies or sample sizes. An earlier draft was partly written by Claude Opus and its token assumption was later corrected. Does not prove the models could execute the full move list.
agent_relevance: Models hold the recursive goal-subgoal algorithm (the MEA core on Hanoi) but should not be asked to enumerate. Have code run the stack and let the model write or fill the rule. Also check solvability before scoring a failure.

source: Khan, Madhavan and Natarajan (2025) A Comment on The Illusion of Thinking: Reframing the Reasoning Cliff as an Agentic Gap (arXiv 2506.18957)
finding: With code tools, a model that called a puzzle impossible in text-only mode handled much larger River Crossing instances. Tool use showed levels: GPT-4o ran a plausible but wrong plan and did not catch it; o4-mini did verify and revise. Cumulative error alone predicts a cliff.
numbers: Hanoi N = 13 needs 8,191 moves; with per-move success 0.9999 the chance of a perfect run is below 45%. A 64,000-token limit at about 8 tokens per move meets the solution length at N = 13. Text-only o4-mini failed 5 pairs with a 3-person boat and called it impossible; tool tests used 20 pairs with a 4-person boat.
quote: the model's inability to perfectly maintain state ... leads it to mistake its own executional limitations for fundamental impossibilities
limits: Few runs per condition, no sample sizes or confidence intervals. Industry authors, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: A model that cannot hold state will declare solvable problems impossible. Keep state in code and treat a model claim of impossibility as a signal to check, not a verdict (G1, G2).

source: Dellibarda Varela et al. (2025) Rethinking the Illusion of Thinking (arXiv 2507.01231)
finding: Replication of Hanoi and River Crossing with incremental stepwise prompting: failures were partly output limits and partly real limits. Reasoning models still stumble at about 8 disks; on solvable River Crossing they solve instances with over 100 agent pairs.
numbers: Abstract only: Hanoi trouble around 8 disks; River Crossing solved with over 100 pairs when instances are solvable. No accuracy tables read.
limits: Only the abstract page was read. Models and sample sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: Splits the verdict: Hanoi is partly a real limit, River Crossing mostly an artifact. Our scaffold should not assume either; test with a solvability check and a code-run solver.

source: Limits of Emergent Reasoning of Large Language Models in Agentic Frameworks for Deterministic Games (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2510.15974)
finding: Giving the model a move-by-move interface with environment feedback did not stop the Hanoi collapse and made it start at lower sizes. Failures looked like loops that reuse earlier continuations.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi up to 8 disks; Claude 3.7 Sonnet (and thinking), DeepSeek V3.1, DeepSeek R1; token budget 30,000. About 40% of the time at n = 8 the model reused previously seen continuations. No exact success rates in the text (figures only).
quote: Access to an environment interface does not delay or eradicate performance collapse
limits: Read through a page-fetch summary. Two model families, one game, single runs, no decoding ablations. The broad mode-following claim goes beyond the data.
agent_relevance: Interaction alone (ReAct-like move-by-move) does not fix a model-held goal stack. The loop needs a code-held stack and a repeated-state check to avoid cycling.

source: Meyerson et al. (2025) Solving a Million-Step LLM Task with Zero Errors (MAKER, arXiv 2511.09030)
finding: Tower of Hanoi with 20 disks (1,048,575 steps) was solved with zero errors by splitting into one-step microagent calls, voting until one answer leads by k, and discarding over-long or misformatted replies.
numbers: gpt-4.1-mini, temperature 0 first vote then 0.1; per-step error about 0.22% at temp 0.1 (0.40% at temp 1.0); k = 3; replies capped at 750 tokens (error rises sharply past about 700 tokens); two independent runs on 10K steps had zero steps wrong in both; projected cost about 3.5K dollars; cost grows as steps times log steps. Other models per-step error: gpt-4.1-nano 0.357, haiku-4.5 0.184, qwen-3 0.234, gpt-oss-20B 0.036.
quote: the system scales log-linearly with s
limits: Read through a page-fetch summary of the first 100k characters. Cost is projected, not billed. The next move is fixed by a known rule and the decomposition was supplied by the harness, not discovered. Votes on one model are not independent in general (G4), although the zero-overlap check was run here.
agent_relevance: Best existing case for code-owned procedure plus tiny model steps. A long goal-subgoal recursion works when the program holds the stack and the model gives one move. It does not show the model can discover the decomposition.

source: Prasad et al. (2024) ADaPT: As-Needed Decomposition and Planning with Language Models (NAACL Findings 2024, arXiv 2311.05772)
finding: Recursive decomposition only when the executor fails (as-needed subgoals, depth cap) beat ReAct, plan-then-execute and Reflexion on three text environments.
numbers: GPT-3.5, max depth 3 (4 on TextCraft). ALFWorld success: ReAct 43.3, Plan-and-Execute 43.3, Try Again 47.8, Reflexion 57.5, ADaPT 71.6. WebShop: ReAct 32.0, Plan-and-Execute 17.0, Reflexion 35.0, LATS 38.0, ADaPT 44.0. TextCraft: ReAct 19.0, Plan-and-Execute 27.0, Reflexion 32.0, ADaPT 52.0. Recipe depth test: depth 2 ReAct 26.9 vs ADaPT 78.2; depth 3 ReAct 1.8 vs ADaPT 38.7. ALFWorld dev, GPT-3.5 executor alone 38.4, with GPT-3.5 planner 58.3; Llama-2-70B executor alone 20.4, with GPT-3.5 planner 43.3.
limits: Read through a page-fetch summary. GPT-3.5 era models. Relies on the executor's own success judgment; on WebShop it overestimates success by over 30 points, stopping decomposition early. Decision tasks only.
agent_relevance: Nearest working LLM-agent form of a goal stack: try, and on failure push a subgoal. It matches G1 (reconsider only on a failure signal). The self-judged failure signal is the weak spot; ours should use a code check.

source: Wang et al. (2026) A Subgoal-driven Framework for Improving Long-Horizon LLM Agents (SGO and MiRA, arXiv 2603.19685)
finding: Online subgoal decomposition with milestone checks raised a strong model's web-task success, and subgoal progress used as reward shaping helped an open model most.
numbers: WebArena-Lite, 165 tasks, pass@1. GPT-4o 13.9%, GPT-4-Turbo 17.6%, Gemini-2.5-pro 23.0% to 32.1% with subgoal prompting. Gemma3 + MiRA 43.0% versus WebRL-trained Llama 38.8% (abstract says 38.4%). Subgoal checker: AUROC 0.84, Kendall tau 0.4585, exact-equivalence F1 0.68 (precision 0.79, recall 0.60). Stuck-midway failures 48.41% to 39.87%; wrong terminations rose 9.52% to 12.03%.
limits: Read through a page-fetch summary of the first part only. The subgoal checker is a proprietary model (Gemini 2.5 pro). Abstract numbers not all visible in tables. Not a pure MEA test.
agent_relevance: Subgoal progress is a usable graded signal (AUROC 0.84) but a poor hard gate (precision 0.79, recall 0.60). Use it as a progress score for S6, not as a pass/fail check (G3).

source: Li et al. (2024) Systematic Analysis of LLM Contributions to Planning: Solver, Verifier, Heuristic (arXiv 2412.09666)
finding: LLMs are poor at producing correct plans and poor verifiers on hard constraints, but better at giving comparative scores to partial plans, which can guide tree search. A heuristic given in the prompt improved ranking.
numbers: Travel planning solver scores below 0.10 for GPT-4o and DeepSeek in direct and CoT settings (for example GPT-4o 0.072 and 0.083; DeepSeek 0.005 and 0.000). Verifier pass rate on travel planning GPT-4o 0.4550 and DeepSeek 0.4890 on a balanced set, barely above chance. GPT-4o feasibility detection up to 61.25% on easy course planning. Heuristic ranking tables show hit@3 commonly 0.74 to 0.92 and comparison accuracy 0.42 to 0.75 depending on model and setting.
limits: Two-column PDF extraction was messy, so heuristic-table cells are approximate. Own benchmarks (travel, course, fitness).
agent_relevance: A model's comparison of two partial states (which is closer to the goal) is more reliable than generating the plan. That is a difference-reduction signal and should be used as a ranker inside code, with length normalizing (G5).

source: Pallagani et al. (2023) Understanding the Capabilities of Large Language Models for Automated Planning (arXiv 2305.16151)
finding: Fine-tuned small code models beat few-shot large models on plan generation across PDDL domains; few-shot large models were low and fell with problem size. Earlier work found Instruct-GPT valid on only 5% of 500 Blocksworld problems.
numbers: Few-shot code-davinci valid-plan rates such as 23.52% / 17.57% falling to 11.89% / 4.69% on harder splits; fine-tuned CodeT5 ranged from 97.52% down to 0.17% depending on split and domain; Instruct-GPT 5% valid on 500 Blocksworld (cited from earlier work).
limits: Table layout was garbled in extraction; column-to-split pairing not fully resolved, so only the pattern is recorded. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Historical baseline. Training on planning data helps in-domain, which is the route we are not taking; a scaffold must supply the structure instead.

source: Veloso, Carbonell, Perez, Borrajo, Fink and Blythe (1995) Integrating Planning and Learning: The PRODIGY Architecture (J. Experimental and Theoretical AI)
finding: Prodigy4.0 is a complete nonlinear planner doing means-ends analysis as backward chaining over goals and operators, interleaved with a forward simulated state (head plan and tail plan). It added learning of control rules to speed up search.
numbers: No benchmark number used here. The paper names goal selection, operator selection and binding choice as the decision points where control knowledge acts, and says its learning aims at search efficiency.
quote: It follows a means-ends analysis backward chaining search procedure reasoning about multiple goals and multiple alternative operators
limits: Architecture survey, not a head-to-head test. Prodigy was later beaten by Graphplan on several domains (c23).
agent_relevance: Gives a clean list of the three decision points a goal stack must expose (which goal, which operator, which binding). In our schema each can be a code-run choice point in S6 with the model proposing and a check selecting.

source: Blum and Furst (1997) Fast Planning Through Planning Graph Analysis (Artificial Intelligence 90)
finding: Graphplan, which builds a layered graph of what is reachable and which actions conflict before searching, solved problems that the means-ends planners Prodigy and UCPOP could not solve within the limit.
numbers: Flat tire problem (at least 12 time steps, 19 actions): Graphplan 1.1 to 1.3 seconds; neither UCPOP nor Prodigy found a solution. Other problems 0.7, 3.4 and 2.8 seconds on a DECstation 2100 against averages of about 90 seconds (range 30 to 2000 s) for compared methods.
limits: 1990s machines and small STRIPS-like domains. Some comparisons ran Prodigy and UCPOP on a faster machine.
agent_relevance: Classical lesson: pure backward means-ends search wastes effort on conflicting goals (mutual exclusion). A cheap compatibility check on subgoals in code before spending model calls prunes dead branches.

source: Automating the Generation of Prompts for LLM-based Action Choice in PDDL Planning (arXiv 2311.09830, ICAPS 2025)
finding: Natural-language prompts made by an LLM from PDDL domains perform like hand-written ones and better than raw PDDL or plain templates. LLM planning lags far behind symbolic planners, but in some domains the best LLM setup scales further than A* with the LM-cut heuristic.
numbers: Abstract page only: no success rates were readable.
quote: Our NL prompts yield better performance than PDDL prompts and simple template-based NL prompts
limits: Abstract-level read only; no tables seen.
agent_relevance: Shows the LLM in the action-choice role inside a classical search loop, the same role as our model filling one operator slot while code holds the search. How the prompt describes operators matters.

source: Large Language Models for Planning: A Comprehensive and Systematic Survey (arXiv 2505.19683) plus the author's own searches
finding: A 2025 survey of LLM planning groups methods into external-module, finetuning and search-style approaches. My searches on 2026-10-25 and 26 for means-ends analysis in LLM agent papers found only one explicit use (MEDAKA, c01); the rest is goal decomposition (c18, c19) or backward chaining for deduction (c04, c06).
numbers: No numbers recorded; survey not read.
limits: The survey appeared in search results only and was not opened. A thin search result is not proof that no other explicit MEA paper exists.
agent_relevance: Gap: explicit difference-reduction prompting for LLMs is thin in the literature. Our own measurement would add new evidence.
